subject: Optimisation tips for a semi-supervised regression

messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Optimisation tips for a semi-supervised regression
parts:
Hi all,

Thanks (to Bob and others) for helping troubleshoot my semi-supervised
regression model. It's now happily running - and when I say "running",
I mean running all weekend and it's only managed 250 iterations (not
out of adaptation yet!).

So I'd like to ask if anyone can spot an optimisation for this model.
It models each observation ("tpor") as a sum of templates, one
template for each class. We have training data where the sparse
pattern of template activation is known, and testing data where it
isn't, and we model them together:

data {
int<lower=2> K; // num classes (88)
int<lower=1> D; // dimensionality of the tpor features (100)
int<lower=1> M_trn; // num training (687)
int<lower=1> M_tst; // num testing (1000)

vector<lower=1e-6,upper=1>[K] proby_trn[M_trn]; // class
activation proby for each instance - for the training data, it's
annotated confidently as patterns of 0.001 and 0.999
vector<lower=-1,upper=1>[D] tpor_trn[M_trn]; // features
vector<lower=-1,upper=1>[D] tpor_tst[M_tst]; // features
}
parameters {
real<lower=1e-6,upper=10> alpha; // concentration
parameter, controlling sparsity for the dirichlet
real<lower=1e-6,upper=10> sigma; // noise stdev
simplex[D] tpl[K]; // template for tpor for class k

// global tendencies for each class to be active (specified as beta params)
vector<lower=0.5,upper=2>[K] tendencies_alpha;
vector<lower=0.5,upper=2>[K] tendencies_beta;

vector<lower=1e-6,upper=1>[K] proby_tst[M_tst]; // as above (see
proby_trn) but this is the thing we want to predict for test data

simplex[K] theta_trn[M_trn]; // mixture parameters
simplex[K] theta_tst[M_tst]; // mixture parameters
}
model {
vector[D] tplsum;

alpha ~ exponential(0.5); // mild-ish prior on the
concentration - don't mind low or high
sigma ~ exponential(2.0); // noise prior, prefer low, want to
encourage the templates to account for the variance
tendencies_alpha ~ exponential(0.5);
tendencies_beta ~ exponential(0.5);

// for each class, there is a global tendency to appear, specified
as a beta distribution.
// for each instance, the global tendencies are sampled to get the
probys for this case.
// the probys are then reinterpreted as weights for dirichlet
sampling the mixture proportions.
// then, the tpor for each obsn is modelled as a mixture of
templates, plus awgn.
for (m in 1:M_trn) {
proby_trn[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);
theta_trn[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_trn[m] * alpha);

tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
for (k in 1:K){
tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_trn[m,k] * tpl[k]);
}
tpor_trn[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);
}
for (m in 1:M_tst) {
proby_tst[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);
theta_tst[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_tst[m] * alpha);

tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
for (k in 1:K){
tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_tst[m,k] * tpl[k]);
}
tpor_tst[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);
}

}


The number of parameters to learn is clearly fairly large (about 200k)
but I believe not off the scale. One thing I wanted to do was
initialise the templates as a simple mean derived from the training
data, but due to stan's strictness about simplexes and floating-point
sums, I had to use flat init. Still, I guess that shouldn't have a
strong effect on the running time of the model, but on its
convergence.

Hints welcome.

Best
Dan

PS an early version with accompanying toy data is at
https://gist.github.com/danstowell/6828740

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimisation tips for a semi-supervised regression
parts:
You can vectorize more, which can sometimes buy you a factor of
2 to 10. But probably not here, because there's a lot else going
on.

The other thing to do is try to figure out some better initial points.
If it's stalled in warmup, it may be struggling to find the high
mass part of the posterior.

I'd try some smaller fake data to make sure it works before setting
off on weekend runs. Is that the toy data set you link below?

I'd also suggest running in parallel if you have more than one core
to spare.

- Bob

P.S. some vectorization hints inline below.

> simplex[K] theta_tst[M_tst]; // mixture parameters
> }
> model {
> vector[D] tplsum;
>
> alpha ~ exponential(0.5); // mild-ish prior on the
> concentration - don't mind low or high
> sigma ~ exponential(2.0); // noise prior, prefer low, want to
> encourage the templates to account for the variance

> proby_trn[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);
> theta_trn[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_trn[m] * alpha);

I'd check that alpha doesn't get too large here. I was having
problems with this kind of parameterization where I saw the
prior count shooting up very high. Andrew also discusses this
in chapter 5 of BDA.

I'd also check that it doesn't get too small, because it wants
to push theta near boundaries, which is probably not where you want
it to go.

> tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
> for (k in 1:K){
> tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_trn[m,k] * tpl[k]);
> }
> tpor_trn[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);

You can replace all this with:

tpor_trn[m] ~ normal(dot_product(theta_trn[m], tpl),

sigma);

> }
> for (m in 1:M_tst) {
> proby_tst[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);

> theta_tst[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_tst[m] * alpha);
>
> tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
> for (k in 1:K){
> tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_tst[m,k] * tpl[k]);
> }
> tpor_tst[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);

This can also use dot_product.

- Bob

Just to note, however, the dot_product() expression doesn't work
because the arguments are [simplex, array of simplexes]*. Writing it
all using matrices rather than simplexes would get me one way of doing
it as a one-liner, but would lose my simplex constraints. Will try and
find a way.

Thanks
Dan

messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Re: Optimisation tips for a semi-supervised regression
parts:
Hi all,

Before optimising, one should make sure one has the right model!
There's a flaw in my model as stated, in that it attempts to model
data in the range [-1,1] as a nonegative sum of templates in the range
[0,1]. (This arose because my data was originally [0,1] before I
decided to add some data reduction.) Not impossible but it would be
making heavy use of the noise term...

After fixing this issue, it is I hope easier to find the posterior
mass - in practice, it is running faster.

Thanks again for the tips, still useful -

Dan

Sorry --- we went over this before. I tried to carefully look
through your types, but messed up.

It'd probably still be faster to copy and then use dot product.
Or adding results to a vector and then calling sum() on that
vector. It vectorizes the sum auto-diff and really speeds things
up. Stan 2 does this automatically with increments to lp__, but
not in other situations.

- Bob

Thanks. Yes indeed - copying my array of vectors ("tpl") into a matrix
allows me to do the multiplication in a single line, and the code goes
about 2x faster. Time to unlearn those intuitions from other
programming languages, about avoiding copying! Since, it turns out,
the effort expended in copying is in this case a minor part of the
budget (as long as we have memory).

Dan

>>> On 10/14/13 4:29 AM, Dan Stowell wrote:
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Hi all,
>>>>
>>>> Thanks (to Bob and others) for helping troubleshoot my semi-supervised
>>>> regression model. It's now happily running - and when I say "running",
>>>> I mean running all weekend and it's only managed 250 iterations (not
>>>> out of adaptation yet!).
>>>>
>>>> So I'd like to ask if anyone can spot an optimisation for this model.
>>>> It models each observation ("tpor") as a sum of templates, one
>>>> template for each class. We have training data where the sparse
>>>> pattern of template activation is known, and testing data where it
>>>> isn't, and we model them together:
>>>>
>>>> data {
>>>> int<lower=2> K; // num classes (88)
>>>> int<lower=1> D; // dimensionality of the tpor features
>>>> (100)
>>>> int<lower=1> M_trn; // num training (687)
>>>> int<lower=1> M_tst; // num testing (1000)
>>>>
>>>> vector<lower=1e-6,upper=1>[K] proby_trn[M_trn]; // class
>>>> activation proby for each instance - for the training data, it's
>>>> annotated confidently as patterns of 0.001 and 0.999
>>>> vector<lower=-1,upper=1>[D] tpor_trn[M_trn]; // features
>>>> vector<lower=-1,upper=1>[D] tpor_tst[M_tst]; // features
>>>> }
>>>> parameters {
>>>> real<lower=1e-6,upper=10> alpha; // concentration
>>>> parameter, controlling sparsity for the dirichlet
>>>> real<lower=1e-6,upper=10> sigma; // noise stdev
>>>> simplex[D] tpl[K]; // template for tpor for class k
>>>>
>>>> // global tendencies for each class to be active (specified as
>>>> beta
>>>> params)
>>>> vector<lower=0.5,upper=2>[K] tendencies_alpha;
>>>> vector<lower=0.5,upper=2>[K] tendencies_beta;
>>>>
>>>> vector<lower=1e-6,upper=1>[K] proby_tst[M_tst]; // as above (see
>>>> proby_trn) but this is the thing we want to predict for test data
>>>>
>>>> simplex[K] theta_trn[M_trn]; // mixture parameters
>>>> simplex[K] theta_tst[M_tst]; // mixture parameters
>>>> }
>>>> model {
>>>> vector[D] tplsum;
>>>>
>>>> alpha ~ exponential(0.5); // mild-ish prior on the
>>>> concentration - don't mind low or high
>>>> sigma ~ exponential(2.0); // noise prior, prefer low, want to
>>>> encourage the templates to account for the variance
>>>> tendencies_alpha ~ exponential(0.5);
>>>> tendencies_beta ~ exponential(0.5);
>>>>
>>>> // for each class, there is a global tendency to appear, specified
>>>> as a beta distribution.
>>>> // for each instance, the global tendencies are sampled to get the
>>>> probys for this case.
>>>> // the probys are then reinterpreted as weights for dirichlet
>>>> sampling the mixture proportions.
>>>> // then, the tpor for each obsn is modelled as a mixture of
>>>> templates, plus awgn.
>>>> for (m in 1:M_trn) {
>>>> proby_trn[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);
>>>> theta_trn[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_trn[m] * alpha);
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> I'd check that alpha doesn't get too large here. I was having
>>> problems with this kind of parameterization where I saw the
>>> prior count shooting up very high. Andrew also discusses this
>>> in chapter 5 of BDA.
>>>
>>> I'd also check that it doesn't get too small, because it wants
>>> to push theta near boundaries, which is probably not where you want
>>> it to go.
>>>
>>>
>>>> tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
>>>> for (k in 1:K){
>>>> tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_trn[m,k] * tpl[k]);
>>>> }
>>>> tpor_trn[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> You can replace all this with:
>>>
>>> tpor_trn[m] ~ normal(dot_product(theta_trn[m], tpl),
>>>
>>> sigma);
>>>
>>>> }
>>>> for (m in 1:M_tst) {
>>>> proby_tst[m] ~ beta(tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta);
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>> theta_tst[m] ~ dirichlet(proby_tst[m] * alpha);
>>>>
>>>> tplsum <- rep_vector(0.0, D);
>>>> for (k in 1:K){
>>>> tplsum <- tplsum + (theta_tst[m,k] * tpl[k]);
>>>> }
>>>> tpor_tst[m] ~ normal(tplsum, sigma);
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> This can also use dot_product.
>>>
>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimisation tips for a semi-supervised regression
parts:
On 10/16/13 6:24 AM, Dan Stowell wrote:
> Thanks. Yes indeed - copying my array of vectors ("tpl") into a matrix
> allows me to do the multiplication in a single line, and the code goes
> about 2x faster. Time to unlearn those intuitions from other
> programming languages, about avoiding copying!

Copying is relatively fast in Stan compared to other operations in
Stan. It's also absolutely fast compared to BUGS/JAGS or R or Python.
In tight loops in Fortran or C++ or Java, you avoid copying because
copying in that context is relatively slow.

> Since, it turns out,
> the effort expended in copying is in this case a minor part of the
> budget (as long as we have memory).

It shouldn't even take that much memory. For a matrix it's
roughly 24 bytes + 8 bytes/cell.

But the real key is that doing this copying is a net savings
in memory because you more than make up in simplified auto-diff
expressions (in both space and time) what you pay in allocating
another matrix.

- Bob
